European Journal of Internal Medicine

Volume status of patients with hyponatremia across the age span - results from a large prospective international study

Varaldo E, Potasso L, Hoorn EJ et al. · 2026 Nov 06
Study Type: Secondary analysis of a prospective international multicentre study (Hyponatremia Intervention Trial, NCT03557957).
Key Question: How do volume status and underlying aetiology of chronic moderate-to-severe hypotonic hyponatraemia vary across adult age groups?
Key Findings:
  • Of 1992 inpatients (median age 73), euvolaemic hyponatraemia predominated (n=1073), mostly SIAD (n=853). Adjusted odds of SIAD were higher at 65-79 years (OR 1.49, 95% CI 1.19-1.88) and ≥80 years (OR 1.47, 95% CI 1.14-1.91) versus <65.
  • Hypervolaemic forms were more frequent at ≥80 years, but this association lost significance after multivariable adjustment.
  • Among hypovolaemic cases (n=613), GI losses dominated in younger patients versus diuretics in ~50% of those ≥80. In hypervolaemic cases (n=306), heart failure rose and liver disease fell with age.
Clinical Relevance: Diuretic-induced hyponatraemia in the very elderly and SIAD across older adults are common in acute medical admissions, supporting early medication review and targeted work-up rather than assumptions based on clinical volume assessment alone.
Limitations: Final volume status was assigned retrospectively from the complete in-hospital course, so it may not reflect the diagnostic uncertainty clinicians face at presentation.

Internal and Emergency Medicine

Unplanned return to hospital from hospital-at-home care: incidence, timing, and determinants

Nicolás D, Parra-Plaza A, Aldea A et al. · 2026 Nov 04
Study Type: Retrospective single-centre cohort study (10,167 HaH episodes, 2021–2025, tertiary academic centre in Spain).
Key Question: How often, when, and why do patients on hospital-at-home (HaH) care require unplanned return to inpatient care, and which factors predict this?
Key Findings:
  • Unplanned escalation occurred in 5.0% of episodes (95% CI 4.6–5.4), at a median of 6 days (IQR 3–12); only 24.6% occurred within 72 h.
  • Respiratory (30.5%) and infectious (18.1%) deterioration were the commonest triggers; one-third of escalations (33.3%) were severe (ICU admission or death).
  • Higher age-adjusted Charlson index (OR 1.11 per point) and early-discharge admission from wards versus direct home admission (OR 1.69; 95% CI 1.25–2.28) were independently associated with escalation; discrimination was modest (AUC 0.68).
Clinical Relevance: As UK virtual wards expand, these data suggest monitoring and safety-netting should extend well beyond the first 72 h, with particular vigilance for respiratory and infective deterioration in comorbid and step-down patients.
Limitations: Single-centre, retrospective design with a modest predictive model limits generalisability to UK virtual ward models and precludes risk stratification for individual patients.

Journal of Hospital Medicine

Things We Do for No Reason™: Routinely withholding IV iron in hospitalized patients with infection

Cool JA, Shi LZ, Freed JA et al. · 2026 Nov 01
Study Type: Commentary/narrative review ("Things We Do for No Reason" series). Not original research; no new data, and the abstract describes no systematic search method.
Key Question: Should IV iron routinely be withheld from hospitalised patients with iron-deficiency anaemia who also have bacterial infection?
Key Findings:
  • The practice of withholding is driven by in vitro evidence that iron supports bacterial growth, not by clinical outcome data.
  • IV iron has established benefit in IDA across several populations (HFrEF, CKD, IBD, malignancy).
  • The authors cite recent data suggesting IV iron does not worsen clinical outcomes in infection (no effect sizes given in the abstract) and conclude it should not be routinely withheld when infection is adequately controlled.
Clinical Relevance: Supports reconsidering blanket deferral of IV iron during acute medical admissions, particularly in HFrEF or CKD patients, though local formulary and trust policy still apply.
Limitations: Abstract does not specify the underlying studies, their design, or how "adequately controlled" infection is defined, so the strength of evidence cannot be judged.

Journal of Hospital Medicine

Time to untether transitional care from hospital quality: Healthcare utilization following discharge from a Department of Veterans Affairs hospital among community-dwelling older persons

Bravata DM, Perkins AJ, Myers LJ et al. · 2026 Nov 03
Study Type: Retrospective observational cohort study (120 US Veterans Affairs hospitals, 2022-23).
Key Question: Does 30-day readmission adequately capture post-discharge outcomes in older adults discharged home after medical or neurological admissions?
Key Findings:
  • Among 99,778 patients aged ≥65, 14.4% had an unplanned readmission by 30 days and 27.5% by 90 days; 71.1% and 49.9% had no acute care use at 30 and 90 days respectively.
  • Mortality was 1.8% at 30 days and 5.6% at 90 days, highest after unplanned readmission (6.1% and 13.1%). Of 30-day deaths, 35.0% occurred without any acute care contact, and 11.2% of 90-day survivors spent ≥10 days in acute care.
  • The authors propose days in acute care within 90 days as a transitional care outcome.
Clinical Relevance: Supports broader post-discharge metrics, including observation stays, ED attendances and acute-care days, when evaluating NHS discharge pathways, rather than relying on 30-day readmission alone.
Limitations: Predominantly male US veteran population within an integrated health system, limiting generalisability to NHS populations; descriptive design with no comparator or causal inference.

American Journal of Medicine

Cervical Spinal Stenosis as an Extracardiac Sentinel for Non-AL Amyloidosis in Older Adults

Wang WT, Wang JP, Huang YC et al. · 2026 Nov 02
Study Type: Retrospective propensity score-matched cohort study (TriNetX global EHR database), with exploratory subgroup analyses.
Key Question: Is cervical spinal stenosis in adults aged 60+ associated with later diagnosis of non-light-chain (non-AL) amyloidosis?
Key Findings:
  • Cervical stenosis carried higher risk of coded non-AL amyloidosis over 7 years versus lumbar stenosis (HR 1.14, 95% CI 1.01–1.29) and versus hip/knee osteoarthritis (HR 1.96, 95% CI 1.70–2.26).
  • Patients with all three features (female, age ≥75, eGFR ≥60) had higher hazards versus osteoarthritis (HR 3.31, 95% CI 2.24–4.87; 2.96 after 1-year landmark) and versus lumbar stenosis (HR 1.85, 95% CI 1.31–2.61). This group was 10.2% of eligible patients but held 16.7% of diagnoses.
  • Absolute risks were not reported.
Clinical Relevance: Cervical stenosis may be a weak prompt to consider ATTR amyloidosis in older patients with unexplained cardiac, neuropathic or other suggestive features, but this does not support screening.
Limitations: Reliance on coded diagnoses in an EHR network risks detection and misclassification bias, and the phenotype is exploratory with no absolute-risk estimates or validation.

American Journal of Medicine

Hepatocellular Jaundice as an Atypical Hepatic Manifestation of Disseminated Gonococcal Infection: A Case Report

Topiwala M, Medisetty MK, Oommen S et al. · 2026 Nov 02
Study Type: Single-patient case report.
Key Question: Can disseminated gonococcal infection (DGI) present with direct hepatocellular liver injury, outside the classical perihepatitis (Fitz-Hugh-Curtis) pattern?
Key Findings:
  • A 46-year-old man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes presented with fever, polyarthralgia, wrist/ankle tenosynovitis, dorsal hand rash, then jaundice with a conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia and raised liver enzymes.
  • Blood cultures grew *N. gonorrhoeae* (urine culture sterile); no high-risk sexual history or genitourinary symptoms were elicited.
  • Ceftriaxone plus doxycycline (chlamydia not excluded) led to rapid improvement and full normalisation of bilirubin and aminotransferases.
Clinical Relevance: Consider DGI in febrile patients with the arthritis-dermatitis syndrome and deranged LFTs even without a sexual history, and send blood cultures and site-specific NAAT, as this could prompt earlier GUM involvement.
Limitations: A single case cannot establish causality; other causes of hepatitis (e.g. viral, drug, diabetes-related) are not clearly excluded in the abstract.

American Journal of Medicine

Enterococci as Emerging Pathogens in Infective Endocarditis and Cardiac Device Infections: Future Implications

Dhand A, Frishman WH · 2026 Nov 07
Study Type: Narrative review. The abstract describes no systematic search methodology.
Key Question: What is the changing epidemiology and clinical significance of enterococci in infective endocarditis and cardiac device infections, and what does this imply for future surveillance?
Key Findings:
  • Enterococci rank among the three leading causes of infective endocarditis, accounting for 15–30% of post-TAVR cases in several registries.
  • *E. faecalis* causes most enterococcal endocarditis (endovascular tropism, biofilm formation, occult endocarditis during bacteraemia). *E. faecium* is flagged as a future threat owing to ampicillin and frequent vancomycin resistance, with mobile resistance elements.
  • Enterococci cause a smaller share of CIED infections but present late, with lead or valve involvement.
Clinical Relevance: With ageing populations and growing TAVR and CIED use, enterococcal bacteraemia in patients with intracardiac hardware warrants a low threshold for echocardiography and early microbiology/cardiology input.
Limitations: No review methods, quantitative synthesis, or treatment recommendations are evident from the abstract; the projected rise in burden is inferential rather than demonstrated.

The BMJ

Perioperative respiratory adverse events in children undergoing adenotonsillectomy with laryngeal mask airway versus endotracheal tube ventilation: multicentre, randomised controlled trial

Han Y, Yi X, Xia J et al. · 2026 Nov 04
Study Type: Multicentre, parallel-group RCT (n=400; four tertiary hospitals, China)
Key Question: Does laryngeal mask airway (LMA) ventilation reduce perioperative respiratory adverse events (PRAEs) compared with endotracheal tube (ETT) in children aged 2-6 years undergoing adenotonsillectomy?
Key Findings:
  • Any PRAE: 22.5% (LMA) vs 57.5% (ETT); absolute risk difference -35.0 percentage points (95% CI -43.5 to -25.7; P<0.001).
  • Benefit was seen intraoperatively (9.0% vs 17.5%) and postoperatively (16.5% vs 49.5%), with less desaturation (15.0% vs 28.0%), airway obstruction (3.5% vs 12.5%), severe cough (10.5% vs 42.0%), and laryngospasm (0% vs 3.0%).
  • Three LMA cases were converted to ETT; no serious adverse events in either group.
Clinical Relevance: Largely applies to paediatric ENT and anaesthetic practice, but is relevant to acute medicine where post-tonsillectomy children may present with respiratory complications or bleeding, and for airway-device reasoning generally.
Limitations: Operators were experienced anaesthesiologists at tertiary centres, and blinding is not described in the abstract, so generalisability to other settings and possible outcome-assessment bias are uncertain.
